label: Curvature Of A Surface
notes: Open by making curvature a surface measurement rather than a decorative word. The unit normal is the first actor: once the surface chooses a consistent normal, bending is read from how that normal changes as the point moves. The slide frames the chapter around measurable objects students can inspect in the notebook.

label: Lecture Route
notes: Use this route slide as the contract for the lecture. Each row pairs a mathematical object with a visual and a numerical check. The goal is to move from the normal vector to the shape operator, then to eigenvalues, trace, determinant, and finally to area distortion under the Gauss map.

label: Normal Orientation
notes: Slow down on orientation. A parametrized surface supplies two tangent directions, and their cross product gives a candidate normal only when the parametrization is regular. The important check is not that the arrow looks plausible, but that it has unit length and is perpendicular to both partial derivatives.

label: Shape Operator
notes: Introduce the shape operator as the tangent part of normal change. If the normal field turns while we move in a tangent direction, the negative derivative records bending in that direction. The minus sign is a convention that makes outward spheres have positive principal curvatures in this deck.

label: From Forms To Matrix
notes: This slide turns the geometric definition into a matrix computation. The first fundamental form measures tangent vectors, the second fundamental form measures normal acceleration, and solving the metric matrix against the second-form matrix gives the linear map whose eigenvalues are principal curvatures.

label: Normal Curvature
notes: Emphasize that normal curvature depends on a direction, not just on the point. The quadratic expression on the unit tangent circle is Euler's formula: the value in direction angle theta is a weighted average of the two principal curvatures. The polar plot makes maxima and minima visible.

label: Principal Directions
notes: Principal directions are the tangent directions in which the shape operator does not shear the direction into another one. Because the operator is self-adjoint for the surface metric, these directions can be chosen orthogonal away from repeated eigenvalues. That is the linear algebra reason curvature lines exist locally.

label: Mean And Gaussian Curvature
notes: Mean and Gaussian curvature compress the same two numbers in different ways. Mean curvature is the average bending and is the quantity that appears in first variation of area. Gaussian curvature is the product and, through the Gauss map, belongs to the intrinsic story as well as the extrinsic one.

label: Example Gallery
notes: Use the example grid to calibrate signs and degeneracies. A plane has no normal change. A sphere bends equally in every direction. A cylinder bends only around its circular direction. A saddle has opposite signs, so its Gaussian curvature is negative even when the surface looks smooth.

label: Umbilics
notes: Umbilic points are where the shape operator is a scalar multiple of the identity. Every tangent direction is principal there, so a direction field cannot choose a favorite axis. On a sphere every point is umbilic; on a general surface the condition is rare and diagnostically important.

label: Gauss Map Area
notes: Present the Gauss map as a map from the surface to the unit sphere of normals. A small patch on the surface is carried to a patch of normal directions, and Gaussian curvature is the signed area scaling in the limiting sense. Positive, zero, and negative curvature correspond to different local behaviors of that normal image.

label: Graph Surface Lab
notes: This slide connects the formulas to the notebook's graph-surface laboratory. From a height function z equals f of u and v, the partial derivatives give the normal, the metric, and the shape operator. The notebook then verifies the unit-normal, self-adjointness, trace, determinant, and sphere tests numerically.

label: Failure Modes
notes: Warn students that a curvature display is only trustworthy after the regularity checks pass. A grid can look fine while the metric determinant is nearly zero, or a sign convention can quietly flip the Gauss map area. Residual panels and ledgers are part of the mathematical explanation, not a programming afterthought.

label: Takeaways
notes: Bring the lecture back to geometric reading. Principal curvature separates directions, mean curvature detects average bending, Gaussian curvature detects signed normal-area distortion, and umbilics mark places where all tangent directions bend equally. Each object has a formula, a picture, and a check.
